title: The Stones Above the Water

plate.narration: Old boundary stones stand above the Great River. Wind bends the grass around their feet. Beyond the wet gravel, a quiet road follows the bank into the foothills.

goal.text: Help the keeper set the river stones right.

steps.label: Stand the lowest river stone up
Pull the new count cord tight
Help the keeper before you leave

stones.narration: You reach the east bank of the Great River. Old boundary stones march up the slope in a crooked row. A dragonling keeper hurries down with a dry cloth. "These hills are called the Red Sky Foothills," she says. "Everyone in one piece? Good. The river shoved my lowest stone out of line last night. Help me set the river stones right, and there will be tea."

markings.narration: She waves one hand, because the other holds a ball of cord. "Two small jobs first. The oldest stone at the top is carved with a mountain and a plume of smoke, and my record board needs a rubbing of it. And my wet river marker slid into the shallows." Her board is full of crossed-out dates. "The numbers never agree. Which job first?"

carving.narration: The oldest stone is taller than the keeper, and grumpier. She tapes damp paper over the carving and hands you charcoal in a rag. "Rub it like you are polishing a pot," she says. "Before the wind wakes up." The grass is already leaning.

rub_check.prompt: Everyone take a corner. Hold the paper flat and rub before the wind lifts it!

rubbed.narration: The rubbing comes off whole: the mountain, the plume, even the tiny chips. "Nobody gets a clean one!" says the keeper. She pegs it on a rock to dry, then squints at the sky in case it is up to something.

rub_torn.narration: The wind snatches the paper and flaps it away like a startled hen. The keeper chases it, then sits on it. What is left has most of a mountain. "Half a mountain is still a mountain," she says.

marker.narration: The river marker is a short stone post with a rope ring on top. It stands in the shallows like a grumpy heron. "Set it where the water reached," says the keeper, "so travelers can see how high it came." She lends you mittens that smell of fish.

marker_haul.prompt: The post is heavy and slick. The strongest hero heaves it up the gravel while everyone else steers and shouts.

marker_set.narration: The post thumps into its hole, high above the wet gravel. The keeper scratches the height on her record board and whistles. "Higher than my grandmother's year! She complained about that one for a month."

marker_slid.narration: The post slides back into the shallows with a rude splash. So you loop its ring over a pole and walk it up the bank together, fish mittens squelching. The keeper hands around her dry cloth again. The post stands. It looks insulted.

row.narration: Nine stones climb the bank like steps for a giant. Each has a notch for one year's highest water, and a ring for the count cord that ties them together. The lowest stone leans toward the river like a sleepy goat. The keeper calls him Splash, which he does not enjoy.

variants.text: Your marker post stands proud at the water's edge.
Your rubbing dries on a rock under a pebble.
Your torn rubbing dries on a rock under a pebble.

plan.narration: Splash is stuck in the clay, leaning as if he might still run off to the sea. The old cord has snapped, and the river is rising again. "He is very heavy and a little proud," says the keeper. How will you stand him up?

lever_check.prompt: Set the pole under Splash and heave until he stands.

trench_check.prompt: Work out which way the trench should run, then dig so Splash slides upright.

smash_check.prompt: Your bigfoot smashes the clay around Splash. Can you steer him upright as he tips?

splash_slip.narration: Splash tips the wrong way and sits down in the shallows. Sploosh! The keeper does not scold. She loops a rope around him, and everyone hauls from the bank. It takes twice as long and half the dignity.

splash_up.narration: Splash stands straight at last. The keeper thanks him. She thanks every stone. Then she freezes. A brown ripple races down the river, carrying branches, a boot and one very surprised duck. "Melt surge!" she says. "Grab everything the river might like!"

surge_check.narration: Up the bank it all goes, fast, hand to hand: the cord, the board, the kettle and the tea things.

interaction.cue: Catch the load, then pass it up the bank to your friend.

onSuccess.narration: Hand to hand to hand, the whole pile climbs the bank.

onFailure.narration: A sock goes one way, a teacup the other, and the surge takes both.

onAssisted.narration: The keeper lends a pair of arms, and the pile climbs the bank.

surge_safe.narration: The surge slaps the gravel and swirls around Splash's feet. Splash stands firm. The duck sails past, quacking its opinion. "Kettle saved," says the keeper. "The river has no idea how to make tea." She gives you a jar of glowing moss. "Mosslight. For work at dusk."

notch_plan.narration: The water left a dark, damp line on Splash: this year's highest. The keeper hands you a chisel the size of a spoon. "Cut the notch right on that line. It will stay for a thousand years. No pressure." How will you cut it?

chisel_check.prompt: The steadiest hands tap the chisel along the damp line while everyone keeps Splash still.

chalk_check.prompt: Chalk the line, check it against the cord, and cut the notch in small, careful steps.

moss_check.prompt: The mosslight shows every grain of the stone. Can you tap the notch along the glowing line?

beat_check.prompt: A humming beat keeps every tap even. Can you swing the mallet to the beat?

notch_cut.narration: The notch comes out clean, with a curl of stone like a ribbon. "That is this year," the keeper says softly. She gives you four coins and a honeycake. "The stone counters up the road pay me in coins. I pay my helpers in cake. Now, a chalk line to check it."

notch_crooked.narration: The notch wobbles like a worm. "Honest," says the keeper at last. "An honest notch." She gives you a leaf for your blistered thumb, then four coins and a honeycake. "The stone counters up the road pay me in coins. I pay my helpers in cake. Now, a chalk line to check it."

chalk_snap.narration: The keeper holds a chalky cord tight from the new notch to the top stone. "One snap shows if the notch sits true. You do it. My arms are tired from being right all day."

interaction.cue: Tap when the chalk cord reaches the gold.

onSuccess.narration: Snap! A chalk line runs straight up the row, right through the notch.

onFailure.narration: The cord snaps her finger instead. "Ow," she says, happily. "True enough."

onAssisted.narration: She holds the cord steady and nods. Snap! The line runs straight through the notch.

cord_plan.narration: The old count cord hangs like a sad noodle, snapped in three places. A new one must run from Splash up through every stone's ring. The keeper hands you a ball of cord as big as a cabbage. "Miss one ring, and the row will whisper about it." How will you thread it?

climb_check.prompt: Scramble up the row and thread the cord through every ring.

throw_check.prompt: Work out the angle, then toss the weighted end through each ring in turn.

wing_check.prompt: Wings lift the cord's end up the row. Can you keep it out of the grass?

cord_tangle.narration: The cord ties itself into a knot as big as a pillow. You pick it apart, loop by loop, while the keeper hands out crackers. By the end, the cord is threaded, and nobody can say who ate the last cracker.

cord_run.narration: The new cord runs through all nine rings, from Splash to the oldest stone. It sags like an empty washing line. "Now pull it tight," says the keeper. "A slack cord tells fibs. Lean uphill, slowly, like you are persuading a cow."

tighten.narration: Everyone takes hold. Lean too hard, and it snaps back. Lean too little, and it sags.

interaction.cue: Lift or lower your end until the cord is steady in the middle.

onSuccess.narration: The cord rises out of the grass, steady as a held breath.

onFailure.narration: The cord wobbles and flops, then slowly comes up as the keeper helps.

onAssisted.narration: The keeper steadies the cord with a claw, and it comes tight.

tight.narration: The cord hums one low note. A beetle rides it all the way to the top, very pleased with itself. "A tight cord is an honest line," says the keeper. "Now the ends, or it will un-hum the moment you let go."

tie_plan.narration: A tight cord is only as good as its knots. If one slips, the line goes slack and the river laughs. The keeper holds out both loose ends. Which knot will you tie?

loop_check.narration: The keeper shows you her loop knot, slowly. You tie both ends, and she checks them.

hitch_check.narration: You wrap each ring twice and pull the hitches snug.

flick_check.narration: Your duskrunner flicks a fast hitch onto the high ring while everyone holds the cord.

tie_good.narration: The keeper tugs the cord. It answers with a tidy twang, like a polite banjo. "That will hold till the river grows up," she says. "Now let us see which stone has been telling fibs."

sight_plan.narration: If any stone leans off the straight cord, someone will see it. The keeper squints along the row and counts nine stones, then ten, then a moth. "Your eyes are fresher than mine," she says. "How will you look?"

sight_check.narration: You crouch beside the keeper and follow the cord with your eyes.

pebble_check.narration: You set a pebble on every stone. One pebble rolls right off.

star_check.narration: Your starweaver draws a line of starlight along the cord. Anything crooked shows at once.

sight_found.narration: There! The fourth stone from the bottom leans out like a sleepy duck. The keeper chalks a big X on it. "Thank you, Splash," she calls, "for being such a good example." Splash says nothing. But he looks smug.

nudge_plan.narration: The fourth stone leans only a little, but it is as big as a bathtub and twice as stubborn. The keeper walks around it like a cat deciding about a box. How will you straighten it?

push_check.prompt: Everyone lean on the fourth stone together. One, two, three, push!

wedge_check.prompt: Find the low side and pack the right stones under it so the fourth stone settles.

brace_check.prompt: Your thornguard braces the fourth stone. Can you pack wedges under it before it creeps back?

fourth_ok.narration: The fourth stone settles with a deep thud. A line of ants marches out from under it, carrying their furniture. All nine stones stand straight along the cord. "Straight!" says the keeper.

fourth_shift.narration: The stone shifts, then settles crooked the other way. "Good enough for today," sighs the keeper. You add one more wedge and pinch a finger. The ants underneath come out to complain, then go back in to complain indoors.

top_stone.narration: You climb to the oldest stone at the top. Its carved mountain looks out over the hills. The keeper lays her record board in the grass. "The notches count the years. The carving shows the old eruption. They should tell one story," she says. "In nine years, I have never caught them agreeing."

variants.text: She holds your rubbing up to the stone, and the little chips line up.
She holds your torn rubbing against the stone to fill the gaps.

stone_order.narration: Near the top, the river has shoved three old stones out of order. The keeper hands out scraps of her notes. "Oldest first," she says. "Read them out. They are mostly tea."

interaction.cue: Share your clues, then put the stones in order, oldest first.
clues: The mossy stone is the oldest of the three.
The carved stone is younger than the notched stone.

onSuccess.narration: Mossy, notched, carved. The three stones sit in their old places.

onFailure.narration: The keeper tuts and fixes the order herself. "The tea got to my notes."

onAssisted.narration: You spread the clues side by side. Mossy, notched, carved.

compare.narration: Two things can be checked before dark. You can count the notches against her record board. Or you can hold the carved mountain up to the real peak on the skyline, which has a flat shoulder like a sleeping cat. Which first?

notch_count_check.prompt: Count the notches from Splash to the top and match each to a date on the board.

peak_check.prompt: Look from the carving to the real peak and back. Where do the shapes agree, and where not?

muddle.narration: The numbers swim, and you lose count three times. "That is how my board got this way," says the keeper cheerfully. She counts with you, notch by notch, until you land on her answer.

clue.narration: Whichever you checked, the answer is the same. The notches add up to one number of years. The board says another. And the carved mountain's shoulder is in the wrong place. On the real peak, it sits farther left. The keeper does not guess why. "One question at a time," she says.

record_plan.narration: The keeper holds her chalk over a clean corner of the board. For once, she does not hurry. "What should I write about the shoulder? I want it true, and I want it small."

wrote_plain.narration: She writes one line: "The carved shoulder and the real one do not match." She does not write why. Then she adds a tiny mountain wearing a hat. "For luck," she says. "The hat is not evidence."

drew_both.narration: She draws the carved mountain and the real peak side by side, with a dotted line between their shoulders. They look like cousins who have never met. "Let the counters decide for themselves," she says.

runner.narration: Boots thump up the slope. A young dragonling runner skids to a stop, red-faced and puffing. "Keeper! The big stone at the counting circle moved in the night! The counters need everyone who can measure!" The keeper looks at her row, then at you. "You have good hands and good eyes. Will you walk with me?"

runner_check.narration: The keeper hands the runner a cup. "She needs a breath before another question." Will you hear the whole story, or just the urgent news so she can rest?

runner_told.narration: The runner catches her breath and tells it in order. The big stone now sits beside a pale, empty hollow, the spot where it used to be. There are no drag marks between them. "It just moved," she says, and sits down on her own feet. "The counters have run out of string."

runner_short.narration: "It moved! No marks!" says the runner, and that is all you ask. You let her rest. "Run, run, run," says the keeper, "then sit, sit, sit. That is the proper order."

go_plan.narration: The keeper hops from foot to foot, which is how she thinks. "The row will keep till morning if it is tied," she says. "But my board must come with me, and I have only two arms." What helps most before you go?

runner_cake.narration: The runner eats the honeycake in three bites, eyes shut. Color comes back to her cheeks. "Best thing," she mumbles, "all day." The keeper beams at you over her head.

carry_board.narration: You tuck the record board under your arm. It is heavier than it looks, full of years that disagree. The keeper locks her toolshed with a key she wears as a necklace. The board hums faintly. Probably the wind. Probably.

tie_off.narration: You pack the chisel and chalk and check Splash's feet one last time. "Back by breakfast," the keeper tells the row. "Behave." Nine stones stand perfectly still.

rest_row.narration: The sun slides toward the hills. "Nobody walks anywhere hungry," says the keeper. She pours tea into cups that do not match. The river hurries by, a little lower than before.

honey_buy.narration: The keeper sells you a honeycake wrapped in a leaf. She drops your coins in a tin like rare beetles. "Honey is the river's opposite," she says. "It stays where you put it."

share_supper.narration: You split your supper with the keeper. She shares hers with Splash by setting a crumb on his head. "Fair is fair," she says, and hangs a river charm around your neck. It smells faintly of fish, like all her gifts.

supper.narration: The keeper tells you the names of all nine stones, and what each did wrong when it was little. The fourth stone once tried to run off to the sea. The tea tastes faintly of river. Nobody minds.

watch.narration: You sit by Splash with your feet near the water. Ants cross his new notch like a bridge. Far upriver, something flashes once in the dusk, then is gone. "Rivers do that," says the keeper. She is wrong, but kindly.

bank_rest.narration: "I walk to the counting circle at first light," says the keeper. "You are welcome to come." A road also follows the east bank to a crossing called Ashspan Bridge. For tonight, there is a warm cup and nine stones in a row.

voiceGuide.tone: Warm, funny, curious, with real consequences. Describe actions and sensory details directly. Short dialogue. Never use "the kind of thing that", "the sort of thing that", or "it was X, the type of thing that makes you Y" comparisons. Let a character act instead of explaining how the reader should feel.
voiceGuide.vocabulary: Read aloud to an eight-year-old. Concrete words, short sentences, distinct voices.
